1.pericope_label: I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth... I sought in mine heart to give myself unto wine, yet acquainting mine heart with wisdom

schools.summary: Ellicott confines himself to glosses — the address is to the heart, the word rendered enjoy is literally see, and the participle acquainting is properly guiding, used of driving an animal or leading a flock, so that what is contemplated is enjoyment controlled by prudence; he takes the closing phrase as the numbered and therefore few days of a life. Delitzsch reads the second verse as an objective judgment rather than an address, takes the participle for raving madness and the man for one who finds pleasure in self-destruction, and glosses the verb of the third verse as spying out.

Gill grants that the faculty of laughter is given for a use and that moderate laughter serves the health of the body and the pleasure of the mind, restricting the censure to laughter at every trivial occasion, which ends in heaviness; he offers a second rendering addressed to laughter itself, and reads the wine of the third verse as good living generally, taken liberally but with sobriety.

Clarke narrows the censure to intemperate pleasure as against sober enjoyment, reads the two clauses as a piece of stagecraft in which laughter and mirth are personified, and says of the third verse that where he had earlier thrown off all restraint he now took the middle course. Wesley makes the move deliberate — disappointed of his hopes from knowledge he resolved on another course — and ends the second verse by challenging all the Epicures in the world to answer it.

Henry supplies the frame: Solomon adjourns out of library and council-chamber into the park and the playhouse, exchanging philosophers and grave senators for the wits and gallants of his court. He calls it a great step downward from the pleasures of the intellect to those of sense, but grants that a thorough trial must knock at this door; and he holds that mirth soberly and seasonably used is a good thing, fitting a man for business and softening the toils of life.

debates.question: How far does the verdict on laughter and mirth reach?

positions.view: Only to excess: the faculty is given for a use, and moderate laughter serves body and mind; what is condemned is laughter poured out on every trivial occasion.
Only to intemperate pleasure, as distinct from any sober enjoyment of the things of this world.
Without softening: the word is one of raving madness, and the man addressed is like one who finds his pleasure in self-destruction.
It is an act of madness fitter for fools than for wise men in this dangerous state of mankind.

debates.question: How much does wisdom govern the experiment with wine?

positions.view: Wholly: the word rendered acquainting means guiding, used of one who drives an animal or leads a flock, so the enjoyment contemplated is controlled by prudence.
Deliberately: where the earlier trial threw off all restraint, this one takes the middle course.
As a mixture — wine and wisdom together — tried to see whether satisfaction could be reached that way.

outliers.note: Supplies a verse paraphrase in which appetite whispers the invitation to turn back from the rugged thorny road of wisdom which so ill repays the toil, and enter pleasure's flowery paths.
Specifies the experiment as an attempt to keep himself and his company always in a merry humour, furnished with every ingenious turn and repartee he could invent or pick up.

themes: I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also is vanity.
I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?

I sought in mine heart to give myself unto wine, yet acquainting mine heart with wisdom; and to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was that good for the sons of men, which they should do under the heaven all the days of their life.

4.pericope_label: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards... Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit

schools.summary: Delitzsch gives the setting rather than the list: a love of wisdom, a sense of the beautiful in nature and art and a striving after splendour were fundamental in Solomon, whose reign was a period of undisturbed peace and whose commonwealth stood at a pinnacle of worldly glory with the attendant danger of being lost in the world; he renders the disputed pair at the eighth verse as mistress and mistresses, and says that of all the enjoyment nothing remained but the feeling of emptiness. Ellicott prefers parks to orchards and traces the word's Persian origin, notes the necessity of tanks where streams dry in summer, and reports that the guesses at the last words of the eighth verse are too numerous to recount and that our version's rendering is by no means among the most probable.

Gill sets Solomon against the emperor who spent his hours catching flies, assumes a herbal garden stocked with everything curious and useful, describes the three reservoirs still shown south of Bethlehem, and holds that Solomon kept within the due bounds of sobriety throughout — so that when he finally sits down to consider what all this cost in expense and toil of mind, he is qualified as few men to give a just estimate.

Clarke fills in the buildings from the histories, doubts that the word behind orchards is native Hebrew at all and points to the Persian and Arabic word from which our paradise descends, lists the attempts at the two dark words of the eighth verse before settling on wives and concubines, and says the labour promised the good he wished for and could not perform the promise. Wesley reads the wood the pools water as nurseries of young trees so many as to make a forest, and takes the claim that wisdom remained as the limited admission that he was not yet wholly seduced from God.

debates.question: What are the two obscure Hebrew words at the end of the eighth verse?

positions.view: Inexplicable on all hands; of the attempts — captives, cups and flagons, cooks and confectioners, a musical form traced to a Phoenician woman — wives and concubines is the likeliest, since these are otherwise unmentioned while music has already been named.
The guesses are too numerous to recount and our version's rendering is by no means among the most probable; concubines is most in favour, though commentators differ over how to justify it.
Rendered without discussion as mistress and mistresses.

debates.question: What does the claim that wisdom remained with him concede?

positions.view: That he kept his judgment through the trial and observed decorum in it, so that the verdict at the end is a competent one.
Only that he was not yet wholly seduced from God — a limited admission, given what is elsewhere reported of his later years.
Not addressed; the interest lies in the extent of the possessions, taxes levied and tribute given, which make the peculiar treasure of kings.

outliers.note: Distinguishes Solomon's undertakings from imperial triviality by setting him against the emperor who spent his hours catching and killing flies.

Supplies a full historical frame absent from the other voices, reading the chapter's catalogue against a reign of undisturbed peace in which the commonwealth stood at a pinnacle of worldly glory with the danger of being lost in the world.

themes: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards:
I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits:
I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees:
I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle above all that were in Jerusalem before me:

I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me.
And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour.
Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.

12.pericope_label: And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly... For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever

schools.summary: Ellicott sets out both readings of the question about the man who comes after the king, and prefers the simpler one — that the phrase means the successor, as it does later in the book, and that the successor can only run the same round already trodden, which fits the theme that in human affairs there is no progress; he also observes that the word until now meaning gain here means profit only, and raises an argument about authorship, that the thought of being forgotten suits Solomon reflecting on himself but not a later writer who had chosen Solomon as his hero. Delitzsch rejects two proposed renderings of the twelfth verse on the ground that the connecting particles are copulative and not correlative, notes the same shift from enduring gain to mere preference, and says the fool is blind although he has eyes and so has as good as none.

Gill treats the return to wisdom as a fresh trial undertaken to see whether something had been overlooked, grants that natural wisdom greatly exceeds folly while holding no true happiness, adds a second and spiritual sense in which the head is Christ and the eyes of the wise are on him alone, and restricts the loss of remembrance to natural wisdom — a wise man is remembered a while, then a brighter genius rises and outshines him, but those truly good and wise are held in everlasting remembrance.

Clarke takes the question as meaning that none can exceed what he has done, since none will ever have such power and means of gratification; he gives the contrast of wise and fool as verse, notes the emphatic repetition in the Hebrew at the fifteenth verse, and draws from it the warning that wisdom is equally subject to the common accidents of life and so cannot make us completely happy. Wesley reads the wise man's eyes as being in their proper place, allows that wisdom is of far greater use than vain pleasures, and points to the wise men of former ages whose very names and monuments are lost.

Henry pictures a man sick of his pleasures and nauseating them, turning back to speculation for a second hearing of a case already tried, so that if the verdict is the same on rehearing the judgment is decisive; no man can expect to find more satisfaction in the world than Solomon did, and the baffled trial need not be repeated.

debates.question: Who is the man that cometh after the king?

positions.view: Any private person attempting the same search: if the king with all his means has failed, there is little likelihood another will do better, and the baffled trial need not be repeated.
The king's literal successor, as the phrase means later in the book; he can only run the same round already trodden, which suits the theme that there is no progress in human affairs.
Neither is argued; the verse is spent rejecting two proposed renderings on the ground that its connecting particles are copulative and not correlative.

debates.question: Is the loss of remembrance absolute?

positions.view: No — the saying is spoken of natural wisdom only; those who are truly good and wise are held in everlasting remembrance.
Yes, as it stands: time sweeps away all remembrance save the few out of millions preserved for a while in the page of history.
The words record the history of Solomon's reflections rather than the book's final conclusions, since the thought suits Solomon himself but not a later writer who had made him his hero.

outliers.note: Uses the sixteenth verse as evidence about the book's authorship, arguing that a writer who had chosen Solomon as his hero for his reputation for wisdom would not have him predict that his wisdom would be forgotten.
Adds a christological sense to the wise man's eyes being in his head, taking the head for Christ, on whom the eyes of the wise are fixed for righteousness and eternal life.

themes: And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly: for what can the man do that cometh after the king? even that which hath been already done.
Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness.
The wise man’s eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all.
Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then I said in my heart, that this also is vanity.
For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; seeing that which now is in the days to come shall all be forgotten. And how dieth the wise man? as the fool.

17.pericope_label: Therefore I hated life... Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me

schools.summary: Delitzsch rejects the ancient renderings that make the work a woeful burden lying upon the speaker in favour of the idiom that makes it evil in his eyes, and draws a conclusion about the book's authorship from the eighteenth verse: a reigning king would not speak so coldly and vaguely of his own son and successor, so the fiction discovers itself here and the speaker is stripped of historical individuality. Ellicott corrects the tense of grievous to the past, denies any special reference to a named heir, and shifts the grievance — the complaint is not so much the hardship of leaving what one has gained as the injustice that the wise man should have no advantage over the fool who enjoys the same without any merit.

Gill will not read the hatred of life simply, since life is God's gift and a blessing so dear that a man will give all he has for it; he takes the words comparatively, of a lessened regard for life beside the lovingkindness of God which is better than life, while reporting that others think Solomon was genuinely weary of it. He preserves the further reading that the labour hated is the writing of books, and that one Jewish commentator applied it to the labour of this book itself, and reports the suspicion that Rehoboam is meant, adding that it proved true.

Clarke reads the plural noun as the lives — of the wise man, the mad man and the fool alike, and equally the stages of a life, child, man and sage — with nothing in any of them worth re-living; he states the reference to Rehoboam as fact and turns it into a reproach, and gives three plain reasons for hating the labour: it did not answer its end, its fruits can be enjoyed only a short time, and it must be left to a man who may be wise, or a knave, or a fool. Wesley says without qualification that his life was a burden to him and that considering human designs increased his discontent, and notes the same opinion about Rehoboam without endorsing it.

Henry treats the turn as a third experiment rather than a conclusion to the second: after a contemplative and a voluptuous life Solomon betook himself to an active one. Business is a thing wise men take pleasure in — they are in their element in it and complain when out of it — so the good a man should do might reasonably be found here. What defeats it is the qualifier: the labour is under the sun, and Henry sets against it a business above the sun which is perpetual blessedness, work done in conformity to God's will as it is done in heaven, which no man has reason to hate or to despair of. He is careful too that the labour hated was the better sort, not the drudgery of hewers of wood and drawers of water but rational business carried on in wisdom, knowledge and equity.

debates.question: Is the heir a particular man?

positions.view: Rehoboam, stated outright and turned into a reproach — the wisest of men left one son to inherit throne and estates, and he was the silliest of fools.
Reported as a suspicion held by some; Gill adds that it proved true in the event.
No special reference; only the general principle that the wisest must leave what his labour gained to another who may be destitute of wisdom.
The very indefiniteness is the evidence: a reigning king would not speak so of his own successor, so the fiction discovers itself and the speaker is stripped of historical individuality.

debates.question: How strongly should the hatred of life be taken?

positions.view: Comparatively only: life is God's gift and a blessing so dear a man will give all he has for it, so what is meant is a lessened regard for it beside the lovingkindness of God.
At full strength: his life was a burden to him, and nothing in any stage of it was worth re-living.
The question is grammatical rather than devotional — not a burden lying upon him but something that appeared evil in his eyes, and in the past tense.

outliers.note: Sets against the labour under the sun a business above the sun which is perpetual blessedness, so that the chapter's despair is confined to work done for the meat that perishes.
Preserves a reading in which the labour Solomon hated is the writing of books, and reports that Aben Ezra applied the verse to the labour of this book itself.

themes: Therefore I hated life; because the work that is wrought under the sun is grievous unto me: for all is vanity and vexation of spirit.
Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me.
And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed myself wise under the sun. This is also vanity.

20.pericope_label: Therefore I went about to cause my heart to despair of all the labour which I took under the sun... There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour

schools.summary: Delitzsch distinguishes the verb of the twentieth verse from its near neighbour — not a clear turning round but a turning away toward something new — corrects the Greek rendering of the third quality in the twenty-first verse from manliness to aptness and its attendant good fortune, says flatly that nothing comes of a man's labour but disagreeableness, reports that the Greek translators and Jerome had a different text at the twenty-fourth verse yielding the contrary of what the book means, and adopts the reading without Him at the twenty-fifth while allowing the traditional text defensible. Ellicott notes that the word than stands in italics so that the Hebrew as it lies reads not good, gives both resulting senses without deciding between them, and agrees that without Him has every appearance of being right.

Gill has Solomon turning about deliberately — dropping his studies, desisting from toilsome works, settling at nothing, to relax his mind — spreads the sorrows over all a man's days from youth upward rather than old age only, records the alternative renderings of the twenty-fourth verse including a rabbinic one that turns the clause into a question, keeps the received text at the twenty-fifth, and insists that what is commended is not the eating of the epicure but a cheerful and thankful use of what God gives; he takes the closing verse as a description of the good man, none being naturally so but only such as grace makes good.

Clarke adds that there is no remedy, thinks the labourer of the twenty-first verse is Solomon and the heir Rehoboam, pictures a life whose heart is not filled with the peace of God as all sorrows and restless nights, turns the counsel of the twenty-fourth verse into verse, and argues at length for the reading without Him from eight manuscripts and the ancient versions, showing that it alone binds the surrounding sentences into one argument. Wesley makes the injustice of the twenty-first verse the point, locates the sleeplessness in perplexing cares, defends the received reading at the twenty-fifth on the ground that Solomon was best placed to answer, and has the sinner given up to insatiable desire so that he leaves his heap to those he least desired.

debates.question: Does the twenty-fifth verse read more than I or without Him?

positions.view: Without Him: the reading of eight of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts with the Greek, Syriac and Arabic; it alone binds the surrounding sentences into one argument.

The same sense, though the traditional text is also defensible; the alternative would have the king claim an unparalleled capacity for enjoyment, a boast standing out of connection with all around it.
More than I, kept as it stands — Solomon was the man best placed to answer whether these things can satisfy of themselves.

debates.question: Does the twenty-fourth verse commend eating and drinking or deny that it is good?

positions.view: Both senses stand open: the word than is supplied, and unemended the verse says instead that it is not good for a man to eat, since even this depends on God.
It commends them, in a cheerful and thankful use of what God gives rather than the eating of the epicure; the alternative renderings are recorded but not adopted.
It commends them, and the counsel is worth expanding: drive off anxious care, let reason curb the passions, enjoy the little the world affords, and look to the giver of the power to use it.
The Greek translators and Jerome worked from a different text whose sense is the direct contrary of the book's meaning.

outliers.note: Preserves a Midrashic reading which takes the labourer of the twenty-first verse to be God rather than a man.
Argues a textual case at the twenty-fifth verse from eight of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts and the ancient versions, and states plainly that he believes the variant to be the true reading.

themes: Therefore I went about to cause my heart to despair of all the labour which I took under the sun.
For there is a man whose labour is in wisdom, and in knowledge, and in equity; yet to a man that hath not laboured therein shall he leave it for his portion. This also is vanity and a great evil.
For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun?
For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.
There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God.
For who can eat, or who else can hasten hereunto, more than I?

For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit.
